newsitem.title: USA: NYMEX electricity futures called steady to higher.
newsitem.headline: NYMEX electricity futures called steady to higher.

text.p: NYMEX electricity futures were called to open steady to higher Thursday after yesterday's losses tied to cool, wet weather in the Southwest, rising spot supply due to unit returns and pending capacity increase on the Pacific Intertie.
"It's just a little bit of a bounce," a West Coast broker said, noting there was no fundamental news behind the market's early firmness.

In over-the-counter activity, September Palo Verde (PV) futures quoted at $29.40-29.80 a megawatt hour (MWh) up from Wednesday's close at $29.18 and September California-Oregon Border (COB) was discussed at $22.50-22.65 a MWh against yesterday's settlement at $22.50.
Day-ahead power prices, in early trading, at PV eased to $31.50-33.25, whiloe those at COB held steady at $19.50-20.00.

In their six- to 10-day forecasts, meteorologists called for cool, fair weather in the Pacific Northwest. They predicted clouds and tropical moisture to keep temperatures in the Southwest below normal through the weekend, followed by more seasonal weather next week.
Spot cash power prices in the Northwest firmed this week on no surplus daily offer from Bonneville Power Administration and slower flows through regional hydroelectric projects.
A 550 megawatt (MW) Jim Bridger coal-fired unit in Wyoming was shut Wednesday due to overheating. No restart date was set.
The 254 MW unit 1 at the Valmy coal-fired power plant in Nevada will likely stay offline until Monday after being shut earlier this week due to a rotor problem.
The 750 MW Four Corners coal-fired unit 5 in New Mexico, shut earlier this month to repair a high pressure generator field, was planned to restart next week.
The 1,221 MW Palo Verde 2 nuclear power unit in Arizona continued to coast down to its September refueling outage. Capacity on the Pacific
Intertie transmission system, the main conduit moving cheap Northwest hydropower to southern California, would be raised by 600 megawatts (MW) to 6,900 MW by Monday.
The Intertie's current 6,300 MW rating will expire today, but the limit would likely be extended if the new 6,900 MW rating is not implemented by then.
